inputs.how_stated: the U score of this nodule as dictated: U1 normal, U2 benign, U3 indeterminate or equivocal, U4 suspicious, U5 malignant. (In a multinodular thyroid the report must also record the score of the most suspicious nodule.)

outcomes.recommendation: Reassuring; FNAC not required unless the patient is at statistically high clinical risk of malignancy. No routine ultrasound follow-up.
caveats: Clinical features linked to a higher probability of malignancy: age under 20 or over 60, a firm nodule, fixation to adjacent structures, rapid growth, vocal cord paralysis, regional lymphadenopathy, previous neck irradiation, family history of thyroid cancer.
Discharge without follow-up applies to asymptomatic nodules with no clinical reason to suspect malignancy.

summary.text: The BTA 2014 U classification grades a thyroid nodule on ultrasound from U1 (normal) to U5 (malignant) to estimate the risk of malignancy and guide FNAC.
U1-U2 are reassuring and do not need FNAC unless the patient is at statistically high clinical risk; U3-U5 should go on to ultrasound-guided FNAC.

The report should describe the nodule's characteristics, give measurements of significant nodules and state the U score; in a multinodular thyroid, record the score of the most suspicious nodule. Note retrosternal extension or tracheal deviation.

locator.section: 4.4 Radiology reporting, ii and iii (Good Practice Points)

definitions.text: A thyroid nodule on ultrasound is a discrete lesion that can be told apart from the adjacent normal thyroid parenchyma.
Taller than wide: the anteroposterior diameter exceeds the transverse diameter (AP > TR) in the axial plane.
Spongiform (honeycomb): microcystic spaces with thin walls making up more than half of the nodule.

In a mixed solid and cystic nodule, assess the solid part: an eccentric solid portion, a non-smooth margin, hypoechogenicity and microcalcification within it are specific signs of malignancy; a taller-than-wide or irregular overall shape also predicts malignancy.

tables.title: Ultrasound features indicative of benign and malignant nodules (Table 4.1)
rows: Spongiform or honeycomb appearance (thin-walled microcystic spaces making up more than half of the nodule)
Purely cystic nodule, or a cystic component containing colloid (hyperechoic foci with a ring-down sign)
Eggshell calcification around the periphery of the nodule
Iso-echoic or mildly hyperechoic relative to normal thyroid, typically with a surrounding hypoechoic halo
Peripheral vascularity on colour or power Doppler
Solid and hypoechoic relative to normal thyroid, which may contain hyperechoic foci (microcalcification)
Irregular margin, intranodular vascularity and no halo
Taller than wide (AP > TR in the axial plane)
Irregular or spiculated margin and taller-than-wide shape both have good positive predictive value
Peripheral eggshell calcification with a broken rim and hypoechoic tissue extending beyond it
Typically hyperechoic and homogeneous with a well-defined halo
Hypoechogenicity and loss of the halo are associated with carcinoma

tables.title: Suggested features for the thyroid ultrasound report (Table 4.3)
rows: FNAC/core biopsy, needle gauge, number of passes, location of nodule biopsied; complications: yes/no

pitfalls.text: No single ultrasound feature is diagnostic: use the signs together, and read them against the patient's clinical picture and any cytology.
Nodule size correlates poorly with malignancy and is not a reliable indicator; the U classification rests on morphology.
When clinical suspicion, cytology and ultrasound appearances disagree, management should be discussed at the MDT.

The guideline does not address thyroid lymphoma or metastases to the thyroid, and is written for adults; in children the general principles of management are similar, but nodules are more likely to be malignant and the threshold for surgery is lower.

pitfalls.text: Nodules found incidentally on CT need clinical evaluation, and usually nothing more; ultrasound is advised for suspicious CT findings (extracapsular extension, tracheal invasion, associated suspicious lymphadenopathy), a high-risk patient or significant clinical concern.
A nodule with focal FDG uptake on PET-CT should have ultrasound and FNAC, unless disseminated disease is found and the prognosis of another malignancy would preclude further investigation.
Any abnormal neck lymph node should undergo FNAC to aid diagnosis and staging.
